# Convert complete or legacy manuscript labels back to the stable internal
# codes used by the Results-section filters. This makes the QMD compatible
# with CSV outputs produced before or after the labels were expanded.
morph_code <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)

  x |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:8th|8|eight|eighth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "eighth"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:9th|9|nine|ninth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "ninth"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:10th|10|ten|tenth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "tenth"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex("\\bfemale(?:s)?\\b", ignore_case = TRUE),
      "female"
    )
}

# Convert internal or legacy morph codes to complete manuscript labels.
# This function accepts labels from old and new CSV outputs.
morph_label <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)

  x |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:8th|8|eight|eighth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "Eighth instar"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:9th|9|nine|ninth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "Ninth instar"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:10th|10|ten|tenth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "Tenth instar"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex("\\bfemale(?:s)?\\b", ignore_case = TRUE),
      "Female"
    )
}

# Apply complete labels to every character or factor column immediately
# before the table is sent to flextable. This is the final safeguard that
# prevents bare labels such as Eighth, ninth, or tenth in any table.
normalize_table_labels <- function(x) {
  x <- as.data.frame(x)

  x[] <- lapply(
    x,
    function(column) {
      if (is.character(column) || is.factor(column)) {
        morph_label(column)
      } else {
        column
      }
    }
  )

  x
}

read_result <- function(filename) {
  readr::read_csv(
    file.path(tables_dir, filename),
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      dplyr::across(
        where(is.character),
        morph_code
      )
    )
}

fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
}

fmt_p <- function(p, digits = 3) {
  if (is.na(p)) return("p = NA")
  if (p < 0.001) return("p < 0.001")
  paste0("p = ", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = digits))
}


# Format manuscript tables for Word with no vertical rules, a rule at the
# top of the table, a rule beneath the column headings, and a closing rule.
manuscript_table <- function(x, align = NULL) {
  x <- normalize_table_labels(x)

  rule <- officer::fp_border(color = "black", width = 0.75)

  ft <- flextable::flextable(x) |>
    flextable::font(fontname = "Times New Roman", part = "all") |>
    flextable::fontsize(size = 12, part = "all") |>
    flextable::border_remove() |>
    flextable::bold(part = "header") |>
    flextable::hline_top(border = rule, part = "header") |>
    flextable::hline_bottom(border = rule, part = "header") |>
    flextable::hline_bottom(border = rule, part = "body") |>
    flextable::autofit() |>
    flextable::set_table_properties(layout = "autofit", width = 1)

  if (!is.null(align)) {
    if (length(align) != ncol(x)) {
      stop("The alignment vector must have one entry per table column.", call. = FALSE)
    }

    # flextable::align() requires full alignment names. Accept common
    # one-letter abbreviations as a convenience, but translate them first.
    align_key <- c(
      l = "left", left = "left",
      c = "center", centre = "center", center = "center",
      r = "right", right = "right",
      j = "justify", justify = "justify"
    )
    align <- unname(align_key[tolower(align)])

    if (anyNA(align)) {
      stop(
        "Table alignment must be one of: left, center, right, or justify.",
        call. = FALSE
      )
    }

    for (j in seq_along(align)) {
      ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = j, align = align[[j]], part = "all")
    }
  }

  ft
}

# Format an F-test from the joint leg ANOVA (columns already renamed in setup).
fmt_f <- function(row, digits = 2) {
  paste0(
    "$F_{", fmt_num(row$num_df, 0), ",", fmt_num(row$den_df, 2), "} = ",
    fmt_num(row$f_value, digits), ", ", fmt_p(row$p_value), "$"
  )
}

# Format an F-test from either nested-model comparison table schema.
fmt_f_nested <- function(row, digits = 2) {
  residual_df <- if ("full_residual_df" %in% names(row)) {
    row$full_residual_df
  } else {
    row$residual_df
  }
  paste0(
    "$F_{", fmt_num(row$numerator_df, 0), ",",
    fmt_num(residual_df, 0), "} = ",
    fmt_num(row$F, digits), ", ", fmt_p(row$p_value), "$"
  )
}

# Format an F-test from a Type III ANOVA table
# (columns: NumDF, DenDF, `F value`, `Pr(>F)`).
fmt_f_anova <- function(row, digits = 2) {
  paste0(
    "$F_{", fmt_num(row$NumDF, 0), ",",
    fmt_num(row$DenDF, 1), "} = ",
    fmt_num(row$`F value`, digits), ", ", fmt_p(row$`Pr(>F)`), "$"
  )
}

get_term <- function(tab, term_name) {
  out <- tab |> filter(.data$term == term_name)
  if (nrow(out) != 1) stop("Could not uniquely locate model term: ", term_name, call. = FALSE)
  out
}

get_vs_female <- function(tab, group_name, leg_name = NULL) {
  out <- tab |>
    filter(
      stringr::str_detect(
        .data$contrast,
        stringr::regex(
          paste0("^", group_name, "\\s*-\\s*female$"),
          ignore_case = TRUE
        )
      )
    )
  if (!is.null(leg_name)) out <- out |> filter(.data$leg == leg_name)
  if (nrow(out) != 1) {
    stop(
      "Could not uniquely locate contrast for ", group_name,
      if (!is.null(leg_name)) paste0(" within ", leg_name) else "",
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }
  out
}

effect_text <- function(row, positive = "longer", negative = "shorter") {
  pct <- row$percent_difference
  direction <- ifelse(pct >= 0, positive, negative)
  paste0(
    fmt_num(abs(pct), 1), "% ", direction,
    " (Holm-adjusted ", fmt_p(row$p.value), ")"
  )
}

group_labels <- c(
  eighth = "Eighth-instar males",
  ninth  = "Ninth-instar males",
  tenth  = "Tenth-instar males"
)

describe_vs_female <- function(
    tab,
    percent_column = "percent_difference",
    positive = "larger",
    negative = "smaller"
) {
  tab <- tab |>
    filter(stringr::str_detect(.data$contrast, "female")) |>
    mutate(
      group_key   = str_trim(str_remove(.data$contrast, "\\s*-\\s*female$")),
      group_label = unname(group_labels[.data$group_key]),
      pct         = .data[[percent_column]],
      direction   = if_else(.data$pct >= 0, positive, negative),
      clause      = paste0(
        .data$group_label, " were ", fmt_num(abs(.data$pct), 1), "% ",
        .data$direction, " than females (Holm-adjusted ",
        map_chr(.data$p.value, fmt_p), ")"
      )
    )
  paste(tab$clause, collapse = "; ")
}

  }

    segment_list,

  )
}

eye_local_trend_col  <- names(eye_local_slopes)[
  str_detect(names(eye_local_slopes), "\\.trend$")][1]
ear_weapon_trend_col <- names(ear_weapon_slopes)[
  str_detect(names(ear_weapon_slopes), "\\.trend$")][1]

# Number of groups with 95% confidence intervals entirely above zero.
ear_local_n_positive <- sum(ear_local_slopes$lower.CL > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
eye_local_n_positive <- sum(eye_local_slopes$lower.CL > 0, na.rm = TRUE)

# Weapon-ear: female slope and male slopes.
ear_weapon_female <- ear_weapon_slopes |> filter(.data$group == "female")

# ── Integration structure ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Dimensionality, ordination and covariance-matrix results are read from the
# upstream stages rather than recomputed, so that a single set of estimates
# is reported throughout.
integration_rank_one       <- read_result("female_reference_rank_one_tests.csv")
integration_parallel       <- read_result("pca_parallel_analysis.csv")
integration_pc_loadings    <- read_result("pca_loadings.csv")
integration_matrix_omnibus <- read_result("covariance_matrix_omnibus_tests.csv")
integration_sign_audit     <- read_result("covariance_sign_audit.csv")
integration_sign_audit_pooled <- read_result("covariance_sign_audit_pooled.csv")
leg_equivalence            <- read_result("leg_intermediacy_equivalence.csv")

# The primary rank-one scenario excludes head size, because head length

rank_one_proportion  <- rank_one_primary$rank_one_fraction[1]
rank_one_p           <- rank_one_primary$p_value[1]

n_integration        <- integration_sign_audit_pooled$n_individuals_total[1]

pc1_variance          <- integration_parallel$variance_percent[1] / 100
pc2_eigenvalue        <- integration_parallel$observed_eigenvalue[2]

  integration_matrix_omnibus$matrix_type == "covariance"][1]

# Abstract

Alternative mating strategies are often defined by differences in weaponry, but they may also involve coordinated changes in locomotory and sensory traits. I tested whether such traits form integrated strategy-specific phenotypes in Wellington tree wētā (*Hemideina crassidens*), whose males mature as genetically polymorphic eighth-, ninth- or tenth-instar morphs that differ in weapon size and mating behaviour. Using field-collected adults, I compared the body-size-adjusted lengths and allometries of all three leg pairs, eye length and tympanic organ area among females and the three male morphs. I also tested whether weapon size covaried with locomotory and sensory investment within groups. At a common body size, relative leg length generally increased from eighth- to tenth-instar males across all leg pairs, with ninth-instar males intermediate. Tenth-instar males also showed greater anterior leg allocation than females, although anterior–posterior allocation differed little among male morphs. Eye and tympanic organ dimensions followed the same male morph gradient: tenth-instar males had the largest sensory structures and eighth-instar males the smallest. These patterns contradicted the prediction that small, actively searching males would invest most in locomotion and sensory detection. Relative weapon size was positively associated with leg length in nearly every group-by-leg combination, and none of the `r sign_total` within-group correlations among the five size-adjusted traits was negative, providing no evidence of a weapon–locomotion trade-off. Because the male morphs differ both in weapon size and in the number of instars completed before maturity, I decomposed each trait's divergence into a per-instar component and an instar-matched weapon component, using females—which mature at the tenth instar without expressing exaggerated weapons—as the instar-matched reference. Both components were supported for every trait, but the weapon component exceeded the per-instar component for the forelegs, midlegs, eyes and tympanic organs, whereas the per-instar component predominated in the hindlegs. A design-weighted rank-one decomposition captured `r fmt_num(100 * rank_one_proportion, 1)`% of group-effect variation, parallel analysis retained `r n_components_retained` component, and permutation tests detected no difference among groups in covariance or correlation structure. Sensory traits were positively associated with their local anatomical substrates. Male weapon–ear slopes did not exclude zero, but the smallest such slope distinguishable from zero at 80% power ranged from `r fmt_num(we_mde_median, 2)` to `r fmt_num(we_mde_worst, 2)`, so these data neither establish near-zero association nor exclude it. Alternative mating strategies in Wellington tree wētā therefore comprise coordinated divergence along one dominant axis of positive covariance, with no detectable trade-offs and no evidence of morph-specific covariance restructuring, rather than uniformly integrated whole-organism phenotypes.

# Introduction

Alternative mating strategies allow males to achieve reproductive success through divergent solutions to mate competition. In many species, large or well-armed males defend females or reproductive resources, whereas smaller males avoid direct contests and obtain matings through sneaking, satellite behaviour or active searching [@gross1996; @shuster2003; @oliveira2008]. These strategies are often associated with conspicuous differences in body size and weaponry, but alternative male phenotypes can differ in many other aspects of morphology, physiology, behaviour, and life history. They are therefore better understood as integrated phenotypes than as otherwise similar males differing only in the exaggerated trait used to classify them [@west-eberhard2003]. Selection should favour coordinated trait combinations that facilitate the behaviour and ecological circumstances associated with each strategy.

Such phenotypic integration may arise because developing one structure affects the resources available to others, or because selection favours the coordinated expression of functionally complementary traits. Exaggerated sexually selected structures can impose developmental or performance costs that are mitigated by corresponding changes in supporting structures—a process termed secondary sexual trait compensation [@tomkins2005; @husak2011]. Alternatively, investment in an exaggerated structure may occur at the expense of other traits when their development competes for a limited pool of resources [@nijhout1998; @emlen2001a; @moczek2004]. A third possibility is that investment in weapons and investment in supporting structures are positively integrated, such that individuals or morphs with larger weapons also invest more in locomotory and sensory traits—an outcome expected when overall phenotypic quality or developmental resources simultaneously elevate multiple traits [@bonduriansky2003; @tomkins2005]. These processes need not be uniform among male morphs. Developmental switches underlying alternative phenotypes can alter covariance among traits, producing morph-specific patterns of integration even when morphs share the same basic anatomical structures [@snell-rood2010; @rohner2020].

Most work on morph-specific integration has focused on weapons and the structures that support their use. In horned dung beetles, for example, horn length is positively integrated with fore- and hindleg morphology, and this integration can be stronger in major than in minor males [@tomkins2005; @rohner2020], consistent with positive co-expression of weapons and supporting structures in the conventional morph. Similarly, male rhinoceros beetles with relatively long horns also have relatively long wings and foretibiae, potentially improving locomotion and leverage during combat, although horn size is unrelated to eye size after accounting for body size [@mccullough2013]. By contrast, in the male-dimorphic stag beetle *Prosopocoilus inclinatus*, weapon size is integrated with eye size in major males but with foreleg length in minor males [@ito2017], suggesting that the traits co-expressed with weaponry can differ between morphs rather than being uniformly larger in the morph with the largest weapons. These findings show that weapon exaggeration can be accompanied by coordinated changes in other traits, but that the pattern and direction of integration need not be predictable from weapon size alone.

Locomotor and sensory traits should be especially relevant to alternative mating strategies because males must both locate mating opportunities and gain access to them. The spatial distribution of receptive females can generate a fundamental contrast between remaining with and defending current mates and searching for additional mates [@shuster2003]. Males that patrol widely or move among defended mating sites may consequently benefit from locomotor structures that enhance movement, whereas males that defend females may benefit from appendages that provide support or leverage during combat. Sensory demands may also differ among strategies, though the direction of morph differences is not predetermined. In the desert bee *Centris pallida*, small males rely primarily on vision for mate detection while large males use chemosensory cues; correspondingly, small males possess relatively larger eyes despite their smaller body size [@barrett2021; @barrett2026], consistent with enhanced sensory investment in the morph that actively searches for mates. However, if conventional males require accurate sensory assessment of rivals or of gallery quality to defend harems effectively, the direction of morph differences in sensory investment could be reversed. Few studies have examined locomotor and sensory traits together within a single species to determine whether such differences represent coordinated phenotypic divergence or trait-specific responses to the demands of each strategy.

The Wellington tree wētā, *Hemideina crassidens*, provides an opportunity to address this question. This flightless, nocturnal orthopteran is harem-polygynous, and females shelter communally in cavities in trees, hereafter galleries. Males use their enlarged heads and mandibles as weapons in contests for control of female-occupied galleries, and males with larger weapons generally have an advantage during escalated fights [@kelly2005a; @kelly2006d; @kelly2010]. Males express three genetically polymorphic, irreversible morphotypes through maturation at the eighth, ninth or tenth juvenile instar [@nason2020; @kelly2024]. Large tenth-instar males possess the most exaggerated weaponry and commonly fight for control of galleries. Small eighth-instar males possess much smaller weapons and may circumvent larger defenders to obtain copulations or search vegetation for undefended females, whereas ninth-instar males exhibit an intermediate strategy that combines fighting and sneaking depending on the social context [@wilson2019; @kelly2025]. The three strategies attain similar average reproductive fitness, consistent with their maintenance as a balanced polymorphism [@nason2020].

Here, I tested whether these alternative male morphotypes differ in the relative expression and allometric scaling of locomotor and sensory traits. I measured fore-, mid-, and hindleg lengths as indices of locomotor morphology, and eye size and the area of the tympanal ears on the foretibiae as indices of visual and auditory investment. Females were included as a non-morphotypic reference group that shares the species’ general locomotor and sensory requirements but does not use enlarged mandibles in competition for mates. I asked whether the three leg pairs show a common allocation pattern among groups, whether particular groups disproportionately invest in specific legs, and whether any anterior-posterior shift in allocation accompanies strategy divergence. Within each group, I also tested whether head size, used here as a proxy for weapon investment, was positively or negatively associated with leg and sensory-trait size after accounting for pronotum length, or showed little detectable association. These phenotypic relationships can reveal patterns consistent with integration or trade-offs, but cannot by themselves establish resource allocation costs or developmental independence.

Previous work on related questions has generally considered a limited set of weapon-associated traits, most often in male-dimorphic systems, and has rarely combined body-size-adjusted comparisons with analyses of allometric scaling and within-morph covariance. By combining body-size-adjusted trait comparisons, group-specific allometry, anterior–posterior leg allocation, local anatomical integration and within-group weapon–trait covariance, this framework distinguishes morphological divergence among strategies from phenotypic covariance within them. Because morph identity in *H. crassidens* is genetically polymorphic rather than induced by nutritional condition, comparisons among morphs are also less confounded by condition-dependent morph expression than in many polyphenic systems. The approach permits a test of whether alternative strategies represent broadly coordinated phenotypes or mosaics of trait-specific modification.

One feature of this system is central to the design. Morph identity is expressed through the number of juvenile instars completed before maturity, so the male morphs differ both in weapon size and in the number of moults undergone. Within males, instar number and weapon expression therefore change together and cannot be separated. Females, however, mature at the tenth instar as tenth-instar males do, but do not express the exaggerated male head and mandibles. Tenth-instar males and females are consequently matched on instar number while differing in weapon expression, which makes the within-tenth-instar comparison the only contrast in this study that holds developmental duration constant. I therefore estimated that contrast jointly with the within-male instar gradient, which decomposes each trait's divergence into a per-instar component and an instar-matched weapon component.

Three hypotheses make contrasting predictions, and they differ not only in which morph should lead but in the structure of covariance the data should reveal.

First, a **searching and detection hypothesis** holds that eighth-instar males—which locate mates by patrolling vegetation and circumventing gallery defenders—face greater locomotory and sensory demands than their gallery-defending counterparts. If morphology tracks those demands, eighth-instar males should possess relatively longer legs and larger sensory structures at a common body size, and weapon size within groups should be decoupled from, or negatively associated with, locomotory and sensory investment.

Second, a **positive-integration hypothesis** holds that morphotypic differences in weapon size reflect broader variation in developmental resources or overall phenotypic quality, such that conventional tenth-instar males simultaneously express larger weapons, longer legs and greater sensory investment. On this view, weapon size should be positively integrated with supporting structures within every group, and this integration should be strongest in the morph with the largest weapons.

Third, a **single growth-axis hypothesis** holds that the three male morphs lie at different points on one common trajectory of post-embryonic growth, so that traits are displaced along that trajectory by the additional instars rather than being remodelled morph by morph. This hypothesis predicts that divergence is concentrated in a single dominant dimension, that size-adjusted covariances among traits are predominantly positive in every group, that covariance structure itself does not differ among groups, and that traits scaling most steeply with instar number show the largest among-morph differences. It also predicts that once instar number is matched, the residual difference between tenth-instar males and females will be smaller than the among-morph gradient for any trait whose divergence is largely attributable to instar number.

These hypotheses are not mutually exclusive, and the first and third make opposite predictions about the sign of within-group weapon–trait covariance. They also differ in the dimensionality of divergence they imply, which marginal comparisons of trait means cannot address. I therefore tested the marginal contrasts and the covariance structure together, and treated the number of dimensions of divergence and the sign and homogeneity of within-group covariance as results in their own right. Group-specific allometric slopes would indicate that trait expression scales differently with body size among morphotypes, whereas differences in elevation with common slopes would indicate proportional shifts in relative investment. Ninth-instar males were expected to be intermediate or more generalized, consistent with their flexible combination of fighting and sneaking, whichever hypothesis holds.


# Methods

## Study site and specimen collection

The final sample comprised 313 adult Wellington tree wētā, *Hemideina crassidens*, haphazardly collected at night from vegetation on Te Pākeka/Maud Island, New Zealand (41°02′ S, 173°54′ E), during March and April 2016. Te Pākeka/Maud Island is a 309-ha scientific reserve in the Marlborough Sounds that is free of introduced mammalian predators.

Individuals were collected from vegetation, which is the microhabitat used by searching males; gallery-occupying males and communally sheltering females are under-represented in such a sample, and collection microhabitat and search effort were not recorded in a form that permits correction. The analysed composition of the three male morphs also differed from both published empirical references for this population. Because morph identity is fixed at maturity and the traits measured do not change after the final moult, these sampling features do not affect the within-individual relationships on which the integration analyses rest. They do, however, limit what the group means represent: they describe the sampled subset of each group rather than each group as a whole, and the direction of any bias cannot be recovered from the archived data.

Following @kelly2010 and @kelly2026, I assigned adult males to eighth-, ninth- or tenth-instar morphotypes using mixture models of head length. I fitted the models in R using the *mixsmsn* package [@prates2013].

Following collection, individuals were euthanized by freezing at $-20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Each specimen was subsequently dissected to remove the head, pronotum, both forelegs, both midlegs and both hindlegs. All structures dissected from an individual were placed together in a labelled screw-cap tube to preserve their association with the individual's unique identifier.

## Digital imaging and morphological measurements

Specimens were transported to the Université du Québec à Montréal, where each dissected structure was photographed separately using a Canon EOS 5D Mark IV digital camera fitted with a Canon EF 100 mm f/2.8L IS USM Macro lens and Canon MT-26EX-RT macro flashes. The camera was mounted on a copy stand approximately 40 cm above the specimen, with the camera sensor parallel to the imaging surface. Each specimen was photographed with its identifier and a ruler positioned in the same plane. Images were calibrated from the ruler, and a visible 5-mm scale bar was added using ImageJ.

Morphological measurements were obtained from the calibrated images using Fiji [@schindelin2012]. All linear traits were measured using the straight-line tool, with measurement endpoints defined by consistent anatomical landmarks illustrated in @fig-morphological-measurements. Ear area was measured by tracing the perimeter of the tympanal membrane using the freehand selection tool.

The measured linear traits were pronotum length, head length, head width, eye length, and the femur and tibia lengths of the forelegs, midlegs and hindlegs. Left and right structures were measured independently for bilateral traits, and the mean of the two sides was used in the analyses. Total foreleg, midleg and hindleg lengths were calculated as the sum of the corresponding femur and tibia lengths.

## Measurement repeatability

Measurement repeatability was assessed using 48 individuals: 12 from each of the four sex or morph groups, with one individual from each of 12 recorded size strata within each group. Every trait was remeasured twice from the original images, yielding three measurements per trait when the original measurement was included. Image order was randomized independently for each measurement round, and previous measurements were not consulted during remeasurement.

Repeatability was estimated separately for each trait using a linear mixed-effects model containing individual identity as a random intercept and no fixed effects. The intraclass correlation coefficient was calculated as the proportion of total variance attributable to differences among individuals:

$$
R =
\frac{V_{\mathrm{individual}}}
     {V_{\mathrm{individual}} + V_{\mathrm{residual}}}.
$$

## Statistical analysis

All analyses were conducted in R [@rcoreteam2025]. Data preparation and visualization were performed using the *tidyverse* [@wickham2019]. Ordinary least-squares models were fitted using base R. The repeated-leg analyses used generalized least squares in *nlme* [@R-nlme]. Estimated marginal means, allometric trends and contrasts were calculated using *emmeans* [@lenth2019package]. Model diagnostics and graphical checks were produced using *performance* [@ludecke2021], *see* [@ludecke2021a] and *broom* [@robinson2014].

Females and eighth-, ninth- and tenth-instar males were represented by the four levels of a categorical variable termed `group`. Pronotum length was used as the measure of structural body size. Composite head size was calculated as the geometric mean of head length and head width:

$$
\mathrm{head\ size}
=
\sqrt{
  \mathrm{head\ length}
  \times
  \mathrm{head\ width}
}.
$$

Because ear size was measured as an area, its square root was taken to express it as a linear dimension before analysis. All continuous morphological variables were then transformed using natural logarithms. Allometric slopes from these log--log models can therefore be interpreted as allometric exponents.

Log pronotum length was centred on a pronotum length of 7.2 mm:

$$
\log P_c
=
\log(\mathrm{pronotum})-\log(7.2).
$$

This reference value lay within the range of pronotum lengths shared by all four groups. Model intercepts and estimated marginal means at $\log P_c=0$ therefore describe individuals with a pronotum length of 7.2 mm and represent interpolation rather than extrapolation.

Before fitting the models, the data were checked for duplicate individual identifiers, unexpected sex or morph labels, missing observations, nonpositive measurements and implausible measurement ranges. Missing observations were excluded separately for each model, so sample sizes could differ among analyses.

### Dimensionality and integration structure

The hypotheses concern the structure of trait integration rather than the marginal size of any one trait, so these structural analyses carry the primary inference about integrated versus mosaic phenotypes. All five non-head traits (foreleg, midleg and hindleg length, linearised tympanal size and eye length) were used together, and composite head size was excluded because head length contributes to male morph assignment. These analyses require a complete data matrix and therefore use the `r n_integration` individuals measured for all five traits.

Divergence among group means was described by a design-weighted rank-one decomposition. Each trait was regressed on log pronotum length with a group interaction, so that group means were compared at a common body size under group-specific allometry, and the three male groups were expressed as female-referenced contrast vectors. This yields a five-trait by three-morph matrix. The best rank-one approximation to that matrix was obtained by singular value decomposition, applying the design weights to the morph dimension, and the proportion of design-weighted group-effect variation captured by the dominant axis was recorded together with the residual variation beyond rank one. A randomization test using `r rank_one_n_perm` permutations of group label assessed whether that residual exceeded what shuffling labels produces. Because "design-weighted" can be defined in more than one defensible way, the rank-one share was recomputed under six alternative weightings and scalings, and the conclusion is reported with that range.

Component retention on the size-adjusted correlation matrix was assessed by parallel analysis. Residuals were taken from group-specific regressions of each log trait on log pronotum length, and a component was retained when its eigenvalue exceeded the 95th percentile of eigenvalues obtained from 1000 random data sets of the same dimension and sample size.

Whether the covariance structure itself differs among groups was tested by comparing within-group covariance and correlation matrices using omnibus and pairwise Frobenius-distance randomization tests, with pairwise p-values adjusted by both Holm and Benjamini--Hochberg procedures. Group labels were not permuted for these tests. Shuffling labels mixes group-specific means into each permuted group, which inflates apparent heterogeneity and makes the observed statistic smaller than almost every permutation; size-adjusted residual vectors were permuted across individuals instead. This preserves exchangeability under the null of equal covariance while retaining the observed group sizes.

Finally, the sign of every within-group covariance among the five size-adjusted traits was audited. Under a strict resource-allocation trade-off at least some of these pairwise covariances should be negative, so the observed number is informative about whether any trade-off is detectable. Bootstrap confidence intervals for the mean within-group correlation were obtained from 2000 resamples of individuals within groups. A positive-sign audit cannot by itself demonstrate the absence of a cost, because variation among individuals in resource acquisition generates positive covariance among costly traits even when those traits compete for allocation during development [@vannoordwijk1986], and this alternative is considered explicitly in the Discussion.

### Leg allometry

Allometric relationships for the forelegs, midlegs and hindlegs were initially examined separately using ordinary least-squares models. For each leg pair, a common-slope model,

$$
\log(\mathrm{leg\ length})
\sim
\log P_c+\mathrm{group},
$$

was compared with a model allowing group-specific slopes,

$$
\log(\mathrm{leg\ length})
\sim
\log P_c\times\mathrm{group}.
$$

Partial $F$-tests comparing the nested models were used to explore whether allometric slopes differed among groups. Group-specific allometric slopes and pairwise differences among slopes were estimated using `emtrends()`. These separate slope analyses are secondary to the repeated-trait model.

The primary test of relative locomotory allocation used a repeated-trait generalized least-squares model. Foreleg, midleg and hindleg measurements were arranged in long format so that each individual contributed as many as three observations. Log leg length was modelled as

$$
\log(\mathrm{leg\ length})
\sim
\log P_c\times\mathrm{group}\times\mathrm{leg}.
$$

Within-individual dependence was represented by an unstructured $3\times3$ residual covariance matrix, with separate residual variances for the three leg pairs and freely estimated pairwise correlations. This structure fitted the data better than heterogeneous compound symmetry (Supplementary Table S10a). The model was fitted by restricted maximum likelihood. Fixed effects were evaluated using type III tests with approximate Satterthwaite denominator degrees of freedom. The three-way interaction tested whether group differences in allometric slope depended on leg identity; because the alternative covariance structure changed this test's conclusion relative to an earlier random-intercept model, individual slope differences were treated as exploratory.

Estimated marginal means were calculated separately for each leg pair at a pronotum length of 7.2 mm. Because the response variables were log-transformed, adjusted means were exponentiated and are reported on the original scale as geometric means. Contrasts were also exponentiated and are reported as ratios, with values greater than one indicating that the first group named in the contrast had the larger predicted trait.

All pairwise group comparisons were calculated within each leg pair. Three biologically motivated contrasts were also evaluated:

1. eighth-instar versus tenth-instar males;
2. ninth-instar males versus the midpoint of eighth- and tenth-instar males; and
3. tenth-instar males versus females.

Additional difference-in-differences contrasts tested whether group differences varied between the foreleg and hindleg, between the midleg and hindleg, and between the mean of the two anterior leg pairs and the hindleg. These contrasts tested differences in relative anterior--posterior allocation rather than differences in absolute leg length alone.

As exploratory secondary analyses, each total-leg pattern was decomposed into its femur and tibia components. Common- and group-specific allometric models were fitted separately to the forefemur, foretibia, midfemur, midtibia, hindfemur, and hindtibia. Nested-model $F$-tests were used to test for group differences in slope, and group-specific slopes were estimated using `emtrends()`. These six separate tests were not used to establish morph-specific allocation in the main repeated-trait analysis.

### Head--leg integration and secondary sexual trait compensation

The secondary sexual trait compensation hypothesis predicts that individuals possessing relatively large heads or weapons should also possess relatively large supporting structures. To test this without treating an estimated head-size residual as a measured predictor, I extended the repeated-trait generalized least-squares model to include raw log composite head size alongside log pronotum length:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(\mathrm{leg\ length}) \sim\;&
\log P_c\times\mathrm{group}\times\mathrm{leg}\\
&+
\log(\mathrm{head\ size})
\times\mathrm{group}\times\mathrm{leg}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The same unstructured within-individual covariance was used. Group- and leg-specific partial slopes relating leg length to head size were estimated using `emtrends()`, controlling for pronotum length. Slopes were compared among groups within each leg pair and among leg pairs within each group. I interpreted a positive slope as positive phenotypic integration consistent with secondary sexual trait compensation, a negative slope as an association consistent with a morphological trade-off, and a slope close to zero as little detectable phenotypic association. The slopes alone cannot establish an underlying resource allocation cost or developmental independence. The earlier residual-index fits are retained only as exploratory analyses, not as the basis of the main weapon–leg inference.

### Body-size-adjusted sensory investment

Group differences in ear and eye investment were examined at a common structural body size. Log-linearised ear size and log eye length were each modelled as functions of log pronotum length, group and their interaction:

$$
\log(\mathrm{sensory\ trait})
\sim
\log P_c\times\mathrm{group}.
$$

For each sensory trait, a common-slope model was compared with the group-specific-slope model using a nested-model $F$-test. Group-specific allometric slopes were estimated using `emtrends()`, and estimated marginal means were calculated at a pronotum length of 7.2 mm.

Eye estimates were exponentiated to return them to the original length scale. For the ear, estimated marginal means on the log-linearised scale were transformed back to the original area scale as

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{ear\ area}}
=
\exp(2\widehat{\mu}),
$$

where $\widehat{\mu}$ is the predicted log-linearised ear size. Contrasts in linearised ear size were squared after exponentiation to obtain ratios on the area scale.

### Local sensory integration

Local association of the ear with the foretibia was tested using raw log foretibia length while controlling for pronotum length and group. The full model was

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(\mathrm{linearised\ ear\ size}) \sim\;&
\log P_c\times\mathrm{group}\\
&+
\log(\mathrm{foretibia})
\times\mathrm{group}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This model tested whether individuals with larger foretibiae for their body size and group also had larger ears. A reduced model containing a common foretibia slope was compared with the full model using a nested-model $F$-test.

Eye--head integration was tested using the corresponding model

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(\mathrm{eye\ length}) \sim\;&
\log P_c\times\mathrm{group}\\
&+
\log(\mathrm{head\ size})
\times\mathrm{group}.
\end{aligned}
$$

I interpreted positive and negative slopes as positive and negative eye–head associations, respectively, and a slope close to zero as little detectable association. Because eyes and weapons share the head capsule, these slopes alone cannot identify developmental integration, an allocation trade-off or developmental independence.

An additional model tested direct covariance between weapon and ear investment:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(\mathrm{linearised\ ear\ size}) \sim\;&
\log P_c\times\mathrm{group}\\
&+
\log(\mathrm{head\ size})
\times\mathrm{group}.
\end{aligned}
$$

I interpreted a negative slope as an association consistent with a weapon–ear trade-off, a positive slope as positive phenotypic integration, and a slope close to zero as little detectable phenotypic association. These slopes do not, by themselves, identify the developmental or resource allocation mechanism.

### Instar-matched decomposition

Because the male morphs differ in instar number as well as in weapon size, the among-morph gradient cannot separate the two. Females mature at the tenth instar, so tenth-instar males and females are matched on instar number and differ in weapon expression. Each log trait was therefore modelled as a function of log pronotum length, a centred instar term (instar number minus ten) and sex:

$$
\log(\mathrm{trait})
\sim
\log P_c+\mathrm{instar}_c+\mathrm{sex}.
$$

With instar centred at ten, the instar coefficient is the per-instar change estimated within males and the sex coefficient is the tenth-instar male-versus-female difference with instar number held constant. The design is not collinear: instar number varies only within males, and sex varies within the tenth instar. The two coefficients were also compared directly, by testing their difference rather than by comparing their p-values, so that the question of which component predominates is answered by a single test.

The same decomposition was fitted jointly across the three leg pairs in one generalized least-squares model,

$$
\log(\mathrm{leg\ length})
\sim
(\log P_c+\mathrm{instar}_c+\mathrm{sex})\times\mathrm{leg},
$$

using the unstructured within-individual covariance and separate residual variances per leg pair described above. This is the multivariate analogue of the per-trait decomposition and respects the non-independence of three legs measured on one individual.

### Precision and minimum detectable effects

A null interaction is only interpretable alongside the smallest effect the design could have detected. For every planned contrast I therefore report the standard error, the 95% confidence interval, and the minimum detectable effect: the smallest true effect detectable with 80% power at $\alpha=0.05$ given the observed standard error and denominator degrees of freedom. These values are given for the planned leg contrasts, for the difference-in-differences allocation contrasts, for the weapon–leg slopes, and for the male weapon–ear slopes. Where a ratio contrast is reported, the minimum detectable effect is expressed as the equivalent percentage difference; for slopes it is expressed in slope units.

### Contrasts and statistical inference

Estimated marginal means and trends are presented with 95% confidence intervals, and denominator degrees of freedom for the generalized least-squares models are reported with each test. Contrast families were defined in advance by the hypothesis each family serves rather than by the table in which a test appears: (i) male-versus-female leg contrasts within each leg pair; (ii) the three morph strategy contrasts within each leg pair; (iii) the anterior–posterior difference-in-differences allocation contrasts; (iv) the per-trait instar and weapon components of the instar-matched decomposition; and (v) the local sensory integration slopes. Holm's sequential procedure was applied within each family.

Tests that fall outside these families are identified as exploratory wherever they are reported and are not used to support the main conclusions. These include the femur and tibia segment models, the group-by-leg slope comparisons, the equivalence-region sensitivities, the multivariate dimensionality and matrix-comparison results reported as a group in the Results, and the cross-analysis multiplicity audit. The exploratory status of the dimensionality analyses reflects their role as descriptions of covariance structure rather than as confirmatory tests of a single pre-specified parameter, not any doubt about the validity of the randomization procedures used. Statistical significance was evaluated at $\alpha=0.05$, but interpretation also considered estimated effect sizes, confidence intervals, the minimum detectable effects and the biological direction of each relationship.

### Model diagnostics

Model assumptions were evaluated using graphical checks of residual normality, homogeneity of variance and relationships between residuals and fitted values. Multicollinearity was assessed using variance-inflation diagnostics. Observations were flagged for further inspection when Cook's distance exceeded $4/n$, leverage exceeded $2p/n$, or the absolute standardized residual exceeded 3, where $n$ was the model sample size and $p$ was the number of estimated coefficients. I used these thresholds only as diagnostic screening criteria and did not automatically delete observations.


# Results

## Sample composition and body-size overlap

The analysis included `r total_n` individuals across the four groups (@tbl-group-summary). Pronotum lengths overlapped from `r fmt_num(common_body_size$common_lower, 2)` to `r fmt_num(common_body_size$common_upper, 2)` mm. The reference pronotum of `r fmt_num(common_body_size$reference_pronotum, 1)` mm used for size-adjusted comparisons therefore lay within the region of common support.


## Dimensionality and integration structure

Because the hypotheses concern the structure of integration rather than the size of any single trait, I first asked how many dimensions the group differences occupy and whether the covariance structure differs among groups.

Across the five non-head traits, the design-weighted rank-one decomposition captured `r fmt_num(100 * rank_one_proportion, 1)`% of group-effect variation (@tbl-integration-structure). The residual beyond the dominant axis was small but still exceeded the permutation distribution (`r fmt_p(rank_one_p)`, `r rank_one_n_perm` permutations), so a detectable second dimension exists alongside the dominant one; it is simply much smaller. The conclusion was insensitive to the definition of the design weighting: across the `r rank_one_n_scenarios` scenarios the rank-one share ranged from `r fmt_num(100 * rank_one_share_min, 1)`% to `r fmt_num(100 * rank_one_share_max, 1)`% (Table S7). Parallel analysis of the size-adjusted correlation matrix retained `r n_components_retained` component, accounting for `r fmt_num(100 * pc1_variance, 1)`% of the size-adjusted variance; the second eigenvalue (`r fmt_num(pc2_eigenvalue, 2)`) fell below its random-data threshold (`r fmt_num(pc2_random, 2)`).

The dominant axis loaded in the same direction on every trait (`r dominant_axis_text`; all PC1 loadings `r ifelse(dominant_axis_all_same_sign, "of the same sign", "with mixed signs")`). Divergence among groups is therefore concentrated in one dimension along which all five traits are displaced together, rather than distributed across several independent trait axes.

Consistent with this, the randomization tests detected no difference among the four groups in within-group covariance structure (`r fmt_p(cov_matrix_p)`) or correlation structure (`r fmt_p(cor_matrix_p)`; `r matrix_permutations` permutations), and no pairwise group comparison survived Holm adjustment (Table S8). Within-group correlations among the five size-adjusted traits were positive in `r sign_positive_total` of `r sign_total` cases, with no negative covariance in any group (@tbl-sign-audit). Mean within-group correlations ranged from `r fmt_num(mean_cor_min, 2)` to `r fmt_num(mean_cor_max, 2)`, and the weakest individual association observed anywhere was `r fmt_num(sign_min_cor, 2)`.

Two conclusions follow, and they frame everything below. First, there is no evidence of a trade-off: not one of the `r sign_total` size-adjusted covariances among these traits was negative. Second, the covariance structure is not remodelled among the morphs. The morphological divergence described in the following sections therefore represents displacement along one shared axis rather than the assembly of morph-specific integrated phenotypes.

## Locomotory morphology

### Relative allocation among leg pairs

The repeated-trait model with unstructured within-individual covariance showed that group differences depended strongly on leg identity (`r fmt_f(leg_group_leg)`). The male developmental groups were therefore not uniformly longer- or shorter-legged than females; the magnitude and direction of group differences varied among foreleg, midleg, and hindleg pairs (@fig-adjusted-traits; Table S14). The body-size-by-group-by-leg interaction was not supported (`r fmt_f(leg_three_way)`), whereas the body-size-by-group interaction was supported (`r fmt_f(leg_size_group)`). Detailed group-by-leg slope comparisons were therefore treated as exploratory.

At a pronotum length of `r fmt_num(common_body_size$reference_pronotum, 1)` mm, eighth-, ninth-, and tenth-instar males had forelegs that were `r effect_text(fore_eighth)`, `r effect_text(fore_ninth)`, and `r effect_text(fore_tenth)`, respectively, than those of females. Midlegs were `r effect_text(mid_eighth)`, `r effect_text(mid_ninth)`, and `r effect_text(mid_tenth)`, respectively. Hindlegs showed a contrasting pattern: eighth-instar males had hindlegs that were `r effect_text(hind_eighth)`, ninth-instar males had hindlegs that were `r effect_text(hind_ninth)`, and tenth-instar males had hindlegs that were `r effect_text(hind_tenth)` relative to females. Overall, foreleg enlargement escalated most strongly at the terminal instar, whereas hindleg morphology followed a shallower trajectory (see below).

The planned strategy contrasts revealed a consistent size gradient among the male morphs. Across all three leg pairs, tenth-instar males had significantly longer legs than eighth-instar males (foreleg: `r fmt_num(abs(strat_eighth_tenth_fore$percent_difference), 1)`% shorter in eighth-instar males, Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(strat_eighth_tenth_fore$p.value)`; hindleg: `r fmt_num(abs(strat_eighth_tenth_hind$percent_difference), 1)`% shorter, Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(strat_eighth_tenth_hind$p.value)`). The ninth-instar estimate lay near the eighth/tenth midpoint; its foreleg midpoint contrast was not statistically different from zero (`r fmt_p(strat_ninth_mid_fore$p.value)`). Two-way equivalence testing supports that reading directly: the ninth-instar midpoint was equivalent to the eighth/tenth midpoint within a $\pm2.5$% margin for all three leg pairs (largest TOST `r fmt_p(leg_equiv_worst_p)`; Table S13). The precision analysis bounds it independently, the smallest difference the design could detect with 80% power being `r fmt_num(midpoint_mde_max, 1)`% against an observed midpoint contrast of at most `r fmt_num(midpoint_obs_max, 1)`% (@tbl-precision-leg). The ninth-instar position is therefore constrained to lie close to the eighth/tenth midpoint for all three leg pairs.

The anterior-posterior allocation analysis tested whether group differences were disproportionate across leg pairs. Among the three male morphs, the planned allocation contrasts were not statistically supported (all Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(alloc_within_male_min_p)` or larger). However, tenth-instar males showed an anterior shift in allocation relative to females: the foreleg-to-hindleg ratio in tenth-instar males exceeded that of females by `r fmt_num(alloc_tenth_female_fore_hind$percent_difference, 1)`% (ratio of ratios = `r fmt_num(alloc_tenth_female_fore_hind$ratio_of_ratios, 2)`, Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(alloc_tenth_female_fore_hind$p.value)`), and all three planned anterior-posterior contrasts were supported (largest Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(max(alloc_tenth_female$p.value))`). This indicates that the locomotory morphology of tenth-instar conventional males is disproportionately weighted toward the anterior leg pairs relative to females.


### Allometric variation

Estimated allometric slopes were below one for every group-by-leg combination, indicating hypoallometric scaling of leg length relative to pronotum length (@fig-leg-allometries; Table S15). Leg allometry was not morph-specific. The body-size-by-group-by-leg interaction was not supported in the better-fitting unstructured covariance model (`r fmt_f(leg_three_way)`), the body-size-by-group interaction was supported (`r fmt_f(leg_size_group)`), and no planned comparison among slopes survived correction. Tenth-instar males had the shallowest point estimates, but the interaction test did not support that ordering, and these slope estimates should not be read as evidence of a morph-specific allometric pattern. The group differences in leg size are therefore more securely described by predicted trait values at a common body size, as above, than by differences in scaling. Exploratory femur and tibia segment tests are reported in Table S16.


## Instar-matched decomposition

Because the male morphs differ in instar number as well as in weapon size, the among-morph gradient above confounds the two. Females mature at the tenth instar, so tenth-instar males and females are matched on instar number while differing in weapon expression. Decomposing each trait into a per-instar component and an instar-matched weapon component separates the contributions of developmental duration and weapon expression (@tbl-instar-decomposition).

Both components were supported for all five traits (per-instar component: every Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(max(instar_decomposition$instar_component_holm_p))` or smaller; weapon component: every Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(max(instar_decomposition$weapon_component_holm_p))` or smaller). Their relative magnitudes differed, however, and the two components differed significantly for every trait (every Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(max(instar_decomposition$component_difference_holm_p))` or smaller).

For the forelegs, midlegs, eyes and tympanic organs the instar-matched weapon component was the larger of the two. Tenth-instar males exceeded same-instar females by `r fmt_num(instar_fore$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1)`%, `r fmt_num(instar_mid$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1)`%, `r fmt_num(instar_eye$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1)`% and `r fmt_num(instar_ear$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1)`% for foreleg, midleg, eye and ear respectively, against per-instar components of `r fmt_num(instar_fore$instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1)`%, `r fmt_num(instar_mid$instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1)`%, `r fmt_num(instar_eye$instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1)`% and `r fmt_num(instar_ear$instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1)`% per instar. The hindleg reversed this pattern, with a per-instar component (`r fmt_num(instar_hind$instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1)`% per instar) that exceeded its weapon component (`r fmt_num(instar_hind$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1)`%).

Fitting the same decomposition jointly across the three leg pairs, with the unstructured within-individual covariance, gave closely similar estimates (per-instar components of `r fmt_num(min(instar_joint_legs$instar_component_pct_per_instar), 1)`–`r fmt_num(max(instar_joint_legs$instar_component_pct_per_instar), 1)`% and weapon components of `r fmt_num(min(instar_joint_legs$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female), 1)`–`r fmt_num(max(instar_joint_legs$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female), 1)`%), so the per-trait and multivariate specifications agree.

This decomposition changes the interpretation of the among-morph gradient. A substantial part of the leg and sensory gradient tracks instar number itself rather than weapon expression. For the hindlegs, essentially all of the apparent divergence among morphs is attributable to instar number: at matched instar the male–female difference was only `r fmt_num(instar_hind$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1)`%, an order of magnitude smaller than the per-instar component. For the forelegs, midlegs, eyes and tympanic organs, by contrast, a difference between tenth-instar males and females of the same instar remains, and it is the larger of the two components. Anterior leg length and sensory investment are therefore where weapon-linked or sex-linked divergence is concentrated, whereas the hindlegs largely follow the general instar trajectory. This also explains why the among-morph contrast obscured the pattern: for the hindleg, the morph gradient and the instar gradient are nearly the same thing.

## Weapon–leg integration

To test whether weapon investment was associated with leg size after body-size adjustment, I fitted log head size alongside pronotum length in the repeated-trait model. The partial association was positive: `r hl_n_positive` of `r hl_n_total` group-by-leg combinations had 95% confidence intervals entirely above zero, and no estimated slope was negative (Table S3). The group-by-leg-by-head interaction was supported (`r fmt_f_anova(hl_int_row)`), indicating heterogeneity in the magnitude of weapon–leg association. The planned morph contrasts among slopes, however, were `r ifelse(hl_strat_all_ns, "uniformly non-significant", "largely non-significant")` after Holm adjustment (Table S4), so they do not establish a simple ranking of morphs by integration strength. These results are consistent with positive phenotypic integration and show no negative weapon–leg association.


## Sensory morphology

### Group differences at a common body size

Ear size (tympanic organ area) and eye length both differed significantly among groups at a common pronotum length. Allometric slopes for ear size on pronotum length did not differ among groups (`r fmt_f_nested(ear_body_test)`), nor did those for eye length (`r fmt_f_nested(eye_body_test)`), justifying a common-slope model for body-size adjustment in both cases.

At a pronotum length of `r fmt_num(common_body_size$reference_pronotum, 1)` mm, tenth-instar males had tympanic organ areas that were `r fmt_num(ear_body_strat_tenth_female$area_percent_difference, 1)`% larger in area than females (Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(ear_body_strat_tenth_female$p.value)`), while eighth-instar males had areas `r fmt_num(abs(ear_body_strat_eighth_tenth$area_percent_difference), 1)`% smaller than tenth-instar males (Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(ear_body_strat_eighth_tenth$p.value)`). The ninth-instar midpoint contrast was not statistically different from zero (`r fmt_p(ear_body_strat_ninth_mid$p.value)`). Eye length showed a larger and more pronounced gradient: tenth-instar males had eyes `r fmt_num(eye_body_strat_tenth_female$percent_difference, 1)`% longer than females (Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(eye_body_strat_tenth_female$p.value)`), while eighth-instar males had eyes `r fmt_num(abs(eye_body_strat_eighth_tenth$percent_difference), 1)`% shorter than tenth-instar males (Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(eye_body_strat_eighth_tenth$p.value)`). The ninth-instar eye midpoint contrast was likewise nonsignificant (`r fmt_p(eye_body_strat_ninth_mid$p.value)`); exploratory equivalence tests are reported in Table S13. In both sensory traits, the morph gradient—from eighth-instar to tenth-instar—paralleled the weapon-size gradient, with tenth-instar males expressing the largest and eighth-instar males the smallest sensory structures (@fig-adjusted-traits; Table S17).


### Local morphological integration

I tested whether ear and eye size covaried with the anatomical structures on which they occur—the foretibia (for the tympanic organ) and the head capsule (for compound eyes)—using one-stage models of raw log traits that included pronotum length and group. The tests did not provide clear evidence that slopes differed among groups for either the ear–foretibia relationship (`r fmt_f_nested(ear_local_test)`) or the eye–head relationship (`r fmt_f_nested(eye_local_test)`). The 95% confidence interval was entirely above zero for `r ear_local_n_positive` of `r nrow(ear_local_slopes)` ear–foretibia slopes and `r eye_local_n_positive` of `r nrow(eye_local_slopes)` eye–head slopes, indicating positive local phenotypic associations in those groups. These tests do not establish that the slopes are equivalent across groups.

The positive eye-head slope deserves particular interpretive attention: because the head capsule is the same structure that bears the mandibular weaponry, weapon size and eye size are necessarily measured on the same structure. Individuals with proportionally larger heads will tend to have larger eyes partly as a geometric consequence of head capsule size, independently of any allocation decision. The eye-head integration slopes (`r fmt_num(min(eye_local_slopes[[eye_local_trend_col]]), 2)`–`r fmt_num(max(eye_local_slopes[[eye_local_trend_col]]), 2)` across groups) should therefore be interpreted as reflecting structural rather than necessarily adaptive coupling between vision and weapon investment.

### Weapon–sensory covariance

To examine within-group weapon–ear covariance, I fitted raw log head size with pronotum length and group in a one-stage model of ear size. The group-by-head interaction was not supported (`r fmt_f_nested(ear_weapon_test)`), providing no clear evidence that the relationship differed among groups. The female slope was positive and its 95% confidence interval excluded zero (`r fmt_num(ear_weapon_female[[ear_weapon_trend_col]], 3)`, 95% CI `r fmt_num(ear_weapon_female$lower.CL, 3)`–`r fmt_num(ear_weapon_female$upper.CL, 3)`, `r fmt_p(ear_weapon_female$p.value)`). The three male slopes ranged from `r fmt_num(min(ear_weapon_slopes[[ear_weapon_trend_col]][ear_weapon_slopes$group != "female"]), 3)` to `r fmt_num(max(ear_weapon_slopes[[ear_weapon_trend_col]][ear_weapon_slopes$group != "female"]), 3)`; none individually excluded zero. However, the exploratory equivalence test did not show that any standardized slope lay entirely within the illustrative near-zero region of ±0.20 (Table S5). Thus these data show no negative weapon–ear association, and they neither establish strong male integration nor demonstrate developmental independence. The precision analysis makes that uncertainty concrete rather than rhetorical. The three male slopes ranged from `r fmt_num(we_male_slope_min, 3)` to `r fmt_num(we_male_slope_max, 3)`, whereas the smallest slope distinguishable from zero with 80% power averaged `r fmt_num(we_mde_mean, 2)` across male morphs and reached `r fmt_num(we_mde_worst, 2)` in the least precise morph. The observed male slopes therefore lie at or below the detection threshold, so these data are uninformative about whether male weapon–ear integration is weak or close to zero. The strength of any positive association in males cannot be estimated from this sample.

## Model diagnostics

Observed and model-predicted trait distributions corresponded closely. Residuals were approximately normally distributed and showed broadly homogeneous variance, with only minor curvature near the extremes of the fitted ranges. Collinearity remained below conventional concern thresholds, and no observation showed sufficient influence to justify exclusion after checking the underlying measurements. I therefore retained the log–log linear models and the repeated-trait generalized least-squares model for inference.

# Discussion

Alternative mating strategies are expected to comprise coordinated combinations of traits that support different routes to reproductive success. The results support that expectation in one respect and reject it in another, and the distinction is what matters here. The searching and detection hypothesis was clearly not supported: at a common body size, eighth-instar males did not possess the longest legs or the largest sensory structures. Instead, relative leg length and sensory dimensions increased from eighth- to tenth-instar males.

What the data do not show is the morph-specific restructuring of integration that a mosaic of trait-specific adjustments would imply. Divergence was concentrated in one dominant dimension that captured `r fmt_num(100 * rank_one_proportion, 1)`% of group-effect variation; all five traits were displaced in the same direction along that axis; not one of the `r sign_total` size-adjusted within-group covariances was negative; and permutation tests detected no difference among the four groups in covariance or correlation structure. The alternative mating strategies of this species are therefore better described as divergence along a single axis of positively covarying traits than as a mosaic of independently modified traits, and that description rests on the covariance structure rather than on the marginal contrasts alone.

The instar-matched decomposition shows further that the axis is not simply a weapon axis. Every trait carries a per-instar component, and an instar-matched weapon component predominates in the forelegs, midlegs, eyes and tympanic organs but not in the hindlegs, where instar number accounts for essentially all of the apparent morph divergence. Head size covaried positively with leg length after controlling for pronotum length, with no evidence of a negative weapon–leg association, and local sensory associations were positive in every group; neither result was accompanied by any evidence that the strength of association differed among morphs.

## Locomotory divergence among mating strategies

The three male morphs formed a consistent gradient in size-adjusted leg length, with tenth-instar males possessing the longest fore-, mid- and hindlegs and eighth-instar males the shortest. Ninth-instar estimates were near the midpoint between the two other male morphs; exploratory equivalence tests are provided in Table S13. This morphological position is consistent with their proposed jack-of-all-trades strategy, in which males can either fight for galleries or circumvent larger competitors depending on the social context [@wilson2019; @kelly2025]. It does not, however, indicate that ninth-instar morphology is specifically adapted for behavioural flexibility. An intermediate phenotype could also arise directly from maturation at an intermediate instar. Functional tests are therefore needed to establish whether the morphological position of ninth-instar males enhances their ability to alternate between fighting and searching tactics.

Comparisons with females revealed a pattern that was not apparent from comparisons among male morphs alone. All male groups had relatively longer forelegs than females, whereas male–female differences in hindleg length varied from negative in eighth-instar males to positive in tenth-instar males. Consequently, tenth-instar males displayed a pronounced anterior shift in leg allocation relative to females. The anterior legs may contribute to stabilizing the body, maintaining purchase on the substrate or manoeuvring during encounters involving the head and mandibles. Such functions would make disproportionate anterior investment particularly valuable to heavily armed, gallery-defending males. Similar reasoning has been applied to the association between horns and foreleg morphology in dung and rhinoceros beetles, where the legs can provide leverage or support during contests [@tomkins2005; @mccullough2013]. Nevertheless, the present data describe morphology rather than mechanical performance, and the proposed role of anterior legs in combat remains untested directly.

The absence of comparable anterior–posterior allocation differences among the three male morphs is also informative. Eighth- and tenth-instar males differ markedly in weapon size and reproductive behaviour, yet they did not exhibit strongly divergent foreleg-to-hindleg allocation after body size was controlled. The primary locomotory distinction among male morphs was therefore a general gradient in the lengths of all three leg pairs rather than a major redistribution of investment from posterior to anterior appendages. A simple distinction between long-legged searching males and anteriorly specialized fighting males is consequently not supported. Instead, the clearest shift in relative leg allocation appears to separate heavily armed tenth-instar males from females, rather than separating conventional and unconventional males.

All leg traits scaled hypoallometrically with pronotum length, meaning that larger individuals within each group possessed proportionally shorter legs. Tenth-instar males generally had the shallowest estimated slopes, but the better-fitting repeated-leg covariance model did not support a body-size-by-group-by-leg interaction. The leg differences among groups are therefore more securely described by predicted trait values at a common body size than by morph-specific slope differences. Weapon allometry in the same population has been reported to differ among male morphs [@kelly2026], but the present exploratory leg-slope estimates do not establish a comparable pattern for locomotory traits.

## Positive weapon–leg integration and its two explanations

Within groups, individuals possessing relatively larger heads generally also possessed relatively longer legs. Eleven of the 12 group-by-leg slopes were clearly positive, and none was negative. These results provide no evidence for the hypothesis that greater investment in weaponry is realized at the expense of locomotory appendages. Instead, they are consistent with positive phenotypic integration between weapons and structures that may support their use. This pattern resembles secondary sexual trait compensation, in which enlargement of a sexual trait is accompanied by enlargement of structures that bear, manoeuvre or otherwise improve the performance of that trait [@tomkins2005; @husak2011].

The present results also resemble those reported for the European earwig (*Forficula auricularia*), another hemimetabolous insect in which male morphs differ in weapon size. @tomkins2005 found positive integration between forceps length and hind-femur length in exaggerated macrolabic males, but no evidence that forceps enlargement traded off against the other measured traits. They proposed that morphological trade-offs may be less readily expressed in hemimetabolous insects than in holometabolous taxa because growth is not confined to a closed pupal developmental system. Wellington tree wētā likewise acquire resources and grow through successive nymphal instars, and the uniformly non-negative weapon–leg relationships are consistent with that hypothesis. This comparison remains tentative, however, because the absence of a negative phenotypic correlation does not rule out an underlying allocation cost. Variation in resource acquisition among individuals can produce positive covariance among costly traits even when those traits compete for resources during development.

Unlike the morph-specific integration observed in European earwigs, the planned comparisons in Wellington tree wētā did not show that weapon–leg integration was consistently stronger in tenth-instar males than in the unconventional morphs. Although the overall group-by-leg-by-weapon interaction indicated heterogeneity among slopes, no planned morph contrast remained clearly supported after correction for multiple comparisons. The positive relationship may therefore reflect a shared developmental architecture linking head and appendage growth rather than a compensatory programme uniquely expressed by heavily armed males. Alternatively, correlational selection in all groups could maintain similar slopes because legs contribute to functions beyond combat, including climbing, foraging, predator avoidance, and mate searching. The evidence is consequently best described as positive phenotypic integration, rather than as proof that longer legs evolved specifically to offset the mechanical costs of larger weapons.

The distinction between resource acquisition and resource allocation is what limits this conclusion most sharply. @vannoordwijk1986 showed that when individuals vary in how much resource they acquire, positive covariance among costly traits is the expected outcome even when those traits compete for the same allocation pool; trade-offs become detectable mainly when acquisition is restricted. In a field-collected sample of adults, variation in acquisition is likely to be substantial and is unmeasured. The complete absence of negative size-adjusted covariances is therefore equally consistent with two readings: a compensatory programme that positively coordinates weapons with supporting structures, and a single growth process in which all traits are elevated together while allocation costs remain present but masked.

The dimensionality and sign results do not separate those two readings, and they weigh against the compensatory reading specifically. Positive integration was present in all four groups rather than concentrated in the most heavily armed morph, and the covariance structure did not differ among groups, which is what a shared growth process predicts and is not what a morph-specific compensatory programme predicts. On the present evidence, positive weapon–leg integration should therefore be described as a property of the common growth axis rather than as evidence for compensation. Separating the two requires either a manipulation of acquisition or estimates of genetic covariance under controlled resource conditions, and that is the most informative experiment the present results point to.

## Sensory divergence among morphs

Sensory morphology showed an especially clear morph gradient. At a common pronotum length, tenth-instar males had the largest eyes and tympanic organs, eighth-instar males had the smallest, and ninth-instar males were intermediate. This pattern is opposite to the prediction that the actively searching eighth-instar morph would invest most heavily in sensory structures used to locate mating opportunities. It also contrasts with the pattern in the desert bee *Centris pallida*, in which small searching males rely more strongly on visual detection and possess relatively larger eyes than large males [@barrett2021; @barrett2026]. Sensory investment therefore cannot be predicted simply from whether a morph searches actively or defends access to females.

A between-sex comparison points to where the searching-and-detection logic may nevertheless hold. At a common body size all three male morphs had longer eyes than females, and ninth- and tenth-instar males had larger tympanic organs, whereas the among-morph ordering ran opposite to the prediction that the actively searching morph invests most in detection. If males are the more mobile sex in this species, then the sensory demand associated with locating mates may be expressed between the sexes rather than among the male morphs. This reading is partly consistent with the *Centris pallida* comparison and partly not: it locates the sensory contrast associated with mate searching at the sex difference while implying that the male tactics do not partition sensory investment in the way that example suggests. The present data cannot test the interpretation directly, because male and female mobility were not measured, but it identifies the between-sex contrast as the more promising place to look for a sensory correlate of searching behaviour, and it cautions against expecting the searching logic to appear as an among-morph ordering.

The greater sensory dimensions of tenth-instar males could reflect demands associated with gallery defence, rival assessment or navigation between refuges and mating opportunities. Alternatively, sensory enlargement may form part of a broader developmental programme associated with delayed maturation and increased weapon expression, without having evolved specifically for the tenth-instar mating strategy. The common sensory allometric slopes favour the latter possibility in at least one respect. Morph differences in eye and ear size reflected shifts in elevation rather than differences in how sensory dimensions increased with body size. Thus, each group followed approximately the same scaling relationship but at a different relative level of sensory expression. Similar elevation shifts can generate substantial sexual- or morph-specific exaggeration without evolving steeper allometric slopes, as recently demonstrated for elongated sensory antennae in crane flies [@hirani2026].

Morphological dimensions alone cannot establish whether these differences translate into sensory performance. Longer eyes might contain more ommatidia, provide greater sensitivity under low light or simply reflect enlargement of the head capsule. Similarly, a larger tympanic membrane could affect auditory sensitivity or frequency response, but membrane area alone does not quantify hearing performance. The present measures are therefore best interpreted as indices of morphological investment rather than direct measures of visual or auditory ability. Physiological measurements of auditory thresholds, eye structure and behavioural responses to visual or acoustic stimuli will be required to determine the functional significance of the observed morphological differences.

## Local sensory integration and weapon–ear covariance

Both sensory structures were positively related to the anatomical structures on which they occur. Individuals with relatively larger foretibiae possessed larger tympanic organs, and individuals with relatively larger heads possessed larger eyes. Neither local relationship showed a clearly supported difference in slope among females and the three male morphs. This pattern is compatible with similar local phenotypic associations across groups, but it does not establish a conserved developmental architecture or exclude biologically meaningful group differences. Such local coupling is unsurprising in the case of the eye because eye dimensions are physically constrained by the size and geometry of the head capsule. The positive eye–head relationship should therefore not be taken as evidence that selection has adaptively coordinated visual investment with weapon enlargement. Some portion of the association is likely to arise mechanically or developmentally because the eye and mandibular apparatus occupy the same structure.

The relationship between weapon and ear investment provides a useful contrast. Tympanic organ area differed substantially among morphs, yet the within-morph weapon–ear slopes in males were imprecise and none individually excluded zero. Importantly, the supplementary equivalence analysis did not establish that these slopes were near zero within its illustrative region (Table S5). The group-by-head interaction was not supported, so a significant female slope alongside nonsignificant male slopes cannot itself be interpreted as a supported female–male difference. The conservative conclusion is that there was no evidence of a negative weapon–ear association, while the strength of positive within-morph integration in males remains uncertain.

This distinction between among-group divergence and within-group covariance is central to interpreting integrated phenotypes. Traits can differ in parallel among morph means without being tightly integrated among individuals within each morph. Conversely, traits can covary strongly within groups even when the magnitude of that covariance does not differ among strategies.
