Recent work on an exaggerated male sensory trait found that substantial sexual divergence can be accompanied by developmental decoupling from the rest of the phenotype [@hirani2026]. The present results do not establish such decoupling in Wellington tree wētā: local sensory associations and weapon–leg slopes were positive, while male weapon–ear covariance was too imprecisely estimated to distinguish weak integration from near-zero association.

## The value of females as a reference

Including females revealed features of male morphology that a male-only analysis would have overlooked. The strongest anterior shift in locomotory allocation involved tenth-instar males relative to females, whereas allocation differences among the male morphs were comparatively small. Females also had smaller eyes than all three male morphs and smaller tympanic organs than ninth- and tenth-instar males at the common body size. These comparisons suggest that some components of the observed morphological gradient reflect male-specific divergence rather than arising solely from the precocial maturation of eighth- and ninth-instar males.

Females should not, however, be treated as an unselected control or as an estimate of the naturally selected optimum. Female legs and sensory structures are subject to their own combination of selection pressures associated with foraging, predator avoidance, reproduction and refuge use. Moreover, females mature at the tenth instar but do not express the exaggerated male head and mandibles. Their inclusion is valuable because they share the general body plan and ecology of males while lacking the same form of weapon-mediated sexual competition, not because their morphology represents a neutral developmental baseline.

The fact that females mature at the tenth instar also gives the female group a second and more specific role. It supplies the only instar-matched comparison available in this system, and that comparison is what makes the decomposition of the among-morph gradient into developmental duration and weapon expression identifiable. Framed this way, the female group is less a control than the design element that makes the decomposition possible. Reading the same contrast as an evolutionary one would be a mistake, because tenth-instar males and females differ in sex as well as in weapon expression. The decomposition is therefore a device for partitioning developmental sources of variance, not a test of selection on weaponry.

## Developmental interpretation of a genetically polymorphic system

The genetically polymorphic expression of the three male strategies strengthens the interpretation of among-morph differences. In many insects with alternative male phenotypes, morph identity depends on nutritional condition, making it difficult to distinguish trait specialization from broad differences in resource acquisition. Wellington tree wētā males raised under common conditions nevertheless mature at different instars and express the corresponding weapon morphologies, indicating that morph identity is not simply induced by poor or favourable nutrition [@kelly2024]. The leg and sensory differences observed here are therefore less likely to be incidental consequences of condition-dependent morph determination.

Genetic control of morph identity does not mean that all morphological divergence is adaptive or environmentally insensitive. Field-collected individuals inevitably differ in developmental conditions, and variation in food, temperature or health could affect the final sizes of weapons, legs and sensory structures within each genetically influenced morph. Moreover, the morphs differ in the number of instars completed before maturity. Some of the morphological gradient may therefore result from heterochrony or from the cumulative developmental effects of additional moults rather than from independent selection on each trait. Body-size adjustment removes the most obvious effect of overall size, but it cannot eliminate developmental-history differences between individuals that reached the same pronotum length through different maturation pathways. Common-garden manipulations that follow multiple traits across successive instars would help separate tactic-specific allocation from general consequences of delayed maturation.

## Limitations and future directions

Several limitations define the scope of inference. First, this study is based on adult morphology and cannot identify the developmental mechanism producing trait covariance. Positive weapon–leg integration might arise through shared hormonal regulation, pleiotropy, genetic covariance, correlated selection or variation in resource acquisition. Second, head size is a biologically relevant proxy for weapon investment but is also associated with feeding and provides the substrate on which the eyes develop. Body-size-adjusted relationships involving head size therefore need not arise solely from selection on the mandibles as weapons. Third, the study did not measure locomotory, fighting or sensory performance. The adaptive value of longer legs, larger eyes and larger tympanic organs remains hypothetical until morphology is linked to functional outcomes. Finally, tenth-instar males were less numerous than the other groups, reducing precision for some morph-specific slopes and making weak interaction effects difficult to interpret; the minimum detectable effects reported with each contrast exist precisely so that these limits are explicit rather than inferred.

The sampling frame also constrains interpretation. Individuals were collected from vegetation rather than from galleries, and the analysed morph composition differed from both published reference compositions for this population. Because morph identity is fixed at maturity and the traits measured do not change after the final moult, this does not affect the within-individual covariance structure that carries the integration inference. It does mean, however, that the group means describe the sampled subsets rather than the morphs as such, and that the absolute magnitude of among-morph divergence could differ in a gallery-based sample. Finally, the decomposition attributes divergence to instar number and to weapon expression without identifying the hormonal or developmental mechanism through which either acts, so the two components should be read as descriptive partitions rather than as causal agents.

The most direct next step is to connect morphological allocation to performance and fitness. Locomotory assays could test whether leg dimensions predict climbing speed, stability or manoeuvrability and whether those relationships differ among strategies. Contest experiments could determine whether anterior leg dimensions improve fighting performance independently of weapon size. Auditory and visual assays could establish whether larger tympanic organs and eyes enhance sensory sensitivity under biologically relevant conditions. Developmental experiments could manipulate resource availability while following genetically assigned morphs across instars, thereby testing whether weapon–leg and local sensory integration are environmentally stable. Finally, estimates of genetic covariance and correlational selection would help distinguish shared developmental regulation from adaptive trait compensation.

## Conclusions

The alternative male strategies of Wellington tree wētā are not simply weapon morphs accompanied by uniformly scaled versions of the remaining phenotype, but nor are they mosaics of independently modified traits. Relative leg and sensory dimensions increased along the eighth- to tenth-instar gradient, and that divergence was concentrated in a single dominant axis on which all five traits were displaced together, with no negative size-adjusted covariance anywhere and no detectable difference in covariance structure among groups. Anterior–posterior leg allocation differed most clearly between tenth-instar males and females rather than among the male strategies, and because tenth-instar males and females are matched on instar number, decomposing the gradient along that contrast shows that the axis combines an instar-number component present in every trait with a weapon component that predominates in the anterior legs and the sensory structures but not in the hindlegs. Head and leg size were positively associated after body-size adjustment, and sensory structures showed positive local anatomical associations, but the strength of weapon–ear covariance within male morphs remains uncertain: the male slopes lie at or below the smallest effect this design could detect, so no conclusion about their magnitude is warranted in either direction.

The two analytic commitments that made these distinctions visible were treating the dimensionality and sign of covariance as results rather than as preliminaries, and using an instar-matched comparison to separate developmental duration from weapon expression. Distinguishing differences among morph means from patterns of covariance within morphs, and both from the developmental time available to each morph, is what allows an alternative mating strategy to be described as integrated, partially integrated, or not integrated at all.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-group-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Sample sizes and descriptive body-size statistics for females and the three male developmental groups."

group_summary |>
  transmute(
    Group              = morph_label(group),
    `Sample size`      = n,
    `Pronotum mean`    = round(pronotum_mean, 2),
    `Pronotum SD`      = round(pronotum_sd, 2),
    `Pronotum minimum` = round(pronotum_min, 2),
    `Pronotum maximum` = round(pronotum_max, 2)
  ) |>
  manuscript_table(align = c("left", "right", "right", "right", "right", "right"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-integration-structure
#| tbl-cap: "Structure of morphological integration among the five non-head traits."

tibble::tibble(
  Quantity = c(
    "Rank-one share of group-effect variation",
    "Range across analysis scenarios",
    "Residual beyond rank one (permutation p)",
    "Components retained (parallel analysis)",
    "Variance explained by the first component",
    "Group difference in covariance matrices (p)",
    "Group difference in correlation matrices (p)",
    "Negative size-adjusted within-group covariances",
    "Traits and groups in the sign audit"
  ),
  Value = c(
    paste0(fmt_num(100 * rank_one_proportion, 1), "%"),
    paste0(fmt_num(100 * rank_one_share_min, 1), "–",
           fmt_num(100 * rank_one_share_max, 1), "%"),
    fmt_p(rank_one_p),
    as.character(n_components_retained),
    paste0(fmt_num(100 * pc1_variance, 1), "%"),
    fmt_p(cov_matrix_p),
    fmt_p(cor_matrix_p),
    paste0(sign_total - sign_positive_total, " of ", sign_total),
    paste0(n_integration_traits, " traits x ", sign_groups, " groups")
  )
) |>
  manuscript_table(align = c("left", "right"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sign-audit
#| tbl-cap: "Within-group correlations among the five size-adjusted traits, by group."

integration_sign_audit |>
  transmute(
    Group                   = morph_label(group),
    `Pairwise correlations` = n_pairwise,
    `Positive`              = n_positive,
    `Negative`              = n_negative,
    `Mean r`                = round(mean_correlation, 2),
    `Median r`              = round(median_correlation, 2),
    `Minimum r`             = round(minimum_correlation, 2),
    `Maximum r`             = round(maximum_correlation, 2)
  ) |>
  manuscript_table(align = c("left", rep("right", 7)))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-instar-decomposition
#| tbl-cap: "Instar-matched decomposition of trait divergence into a per-instar component and a weapon component, estimated within the tenth instar."

instar_display_names <- c(
  foreleg = "Foreleg length",
  midleg  = "Midleg length",
  hindleg = "Hindleg length",
  ear_lin = "Tympanic organ size",
  eye     = "Eye length"
)

instar_decomposition |>
  transmute(
    Trait          = instar_display_names[trait],
    `n`            = n,
    `Per instar (%)` = round(instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1),
    `Per instar P`   = ifelse(instar_component_holm_p < 0.001, "<0.001",
                              sprintf("%.3f", instar_component_holm_p)),
    `Weapon (%)`     = round(weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1),
    `Weapon P`       = ifelse(weapon_component_holm_p < 0.001, "<0.001",
                              sprintf("%.3f", weapon_component_holm_p)),
    `Component difference P` = ifelse(component_difference_holm_p < 0.001, "<0.001",
                                      sprintf("%.3f", component_difference_holm_p)),
    `Larger component` = ifelse(component_difference_log < 0,
                                "Weapon", "Per instar")
  ) |>
  manuscript_table(align = c("left", rep("right", 7)))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-precision-leg
#| tbl-cap: "Planned contrasts in body-size-adjusted leg length with their minimum detectable effects. Differences are expressed relative to the first-named group, except for the difference-in-differences contrasts, which are ratio-of-ratios comparisons."

precision_leg |>
  mutate(
    Leg = if_else(
      is.na(leg),
      "All (allocation)",
      as.character(leg)
    )
  ) |>
  transmute(
    Leg            = Leg,
    Contrast       = contrast,
    `Difference (%)` = round(percent_difference, 1),
    `95% CI`       = paste0(fmt_num(ci_lower, 2), "–", fmt_num(ci_upper, 2)),
    `Minimum detectable (%)` = round(min_detectable_percent, 1)
  ) |>
  manuscript_table(align = c("left", "left", "right", "right", "right"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-weapon-ear-precision
#| tbl-cap: "Within-group weapon–ear slopes and the smallest slope distinguishable from zero with 80% power."

precision_we_slopes |>
  transmute(
    Group                   = morph_label(group),
    `Weapon–ear slope`      = round(weapon_ear_slope, 3),
    `SE`                    = round(SE, 3),
    `95% CI`                = paste0(fmt_num(ci_lower, 2), "–", fmt_num(ci_upper, 2)),
    `Excludes zero`         = ifelse(excludes_zero, "yes", "no"),
    `Minimum detectable slope` = round(min_detectable_slope, 2)
  ) |>
  manuscript_table(align = c("left", rep("right", 5)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-adjusted-traits
#| fig-cap: "Body-size-adjusted predicted lengths of the three leg pairs and eye, and predicted tympanic organ area, for females and the three male morphotypes at a pronotum length of 7.2 mm. Points are model estimates; bars are 95% confidence intervals. Scales differ among panels, and tympanic organ area is in square millimetres."
#| out-width: "100%"

adjusted_trait_plot <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  adjusted_leg_means |>
    dplyr::transmute(group, trait = paste0(leg, " length (mm)"),
                     estimate = predicted, lower, upper),
  ear_body_means |>
    dplyr::transmute(group, trait = "Tympanic organ\narea (mm²)",
                     estimate = predicted_ear_area,
                     lower = ear_area_lower, upper = ear_area_upper),
  eye_body_means |>
    dplyr::transmute(group, trait = "Eye length (mm)",
                     estimate = predicted_eye_length,
                     lower = eye_lower, upper = eye_upper)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    group = factor(group, levels = c("female", "eighth", "ninth", "tenth"),
                   labels = c("Female", "Eighth", "Ninth", "Tenth")),
    trait = factor(trait, levels = c(
      "Foreleg length (mm)", "Midleg length (mm)",
      "Hindleg length (mm)", "Tympanic organ\narea (mm²)",
      "Eye length (mm)"
    ))
  )

ggplot2::ggplot(adjusted_trait_plot, ggplot2::aes(x = group, y = estimate)) +
  ggplot2::geom_pointrange(ggplot2::aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper)) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ trait, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Group", y = "Predicted trait size") +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    strip.background = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```
